issues.body:
## Summary

Writing the same text into a fresh store twice does not always store the same
`admission_score`. The value differs in its last few digits, in about 1 run out
of 10. Nothing about the input changes: same command, same flags, same binary,
same category, empty bank each time.

Because `admission_score` feeds the retrieval importance boost
(`crates/clio-retrieve/src/hybrid_rank.rs:68-70`), two stores that hold
byte-identical content can return different fused `recall` scores, and items
whose scores differ only in those last digits can swap places.

## Cause

Not confirmed. The differing values sit at f32 precision
(`0.7582352941176471` vs `0.7582352169571681`), so the admission path is
probably summing or comparing embedding-derived values in a way whose result
depends on iteration or accumulation order. `novelty_jaccard` in
`crates/clio-admission/src/factors.rs:130-140` uses `BTreeSet` plus `f64::max`
and is order-independent, so the variance is more likely upstream of it, in the
offline embedder or in how candidate factors are combined. That part is not
verified.

## Reproduction

```bash
cargo build --locked --bin clio

T1="The staging deploy retries on ECONNRESET with exponential backoff"
T2="Postgres ts_rank_cd scoring differs from sqlite bm25 ranking"
T3="Reciprocal rank fusion uses k equal to sixty"
T4="Unrelated note about gardening and tomato varieties"

for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  db=/tmp/admx$i.db; rm -f $db
  for t in "$T1" "$T2" "$T3" "$T4"; do
    ./target/debug/clio --db $db --backend sqlite --bank cmpbank \
      remember "$t" --category task_spec >/dev/null 2>&1
  done
done

python3 - <<'PY'
import sqlite3, collections
c = collections.Counter()
for i in range(1, 21):
    con = sqlite3.connect(f"/tmp/admx{i}.db")
    vals = tuple(sorted(r[0] for r in con.execute("SELECT admission_score FROM items")))
    con.close()
    c[vals] += 1
for v, n in sorted(c.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    print(f"{n}x  {list(v)}")
PY
```

## Expected

Identical input into an empty bank should always produce an identical
`admission_score`, so that a stored store returns reproducible `recall` scores.

## Actual

Two distinct values for the same item, roughly 1 run in 10:

```
18x  [0.7582352941176471, 0.7700000000000001, 0.7700000000000001, 0.7700000000000001]
2x   [0.7582352169571681, 0.7700000000000001, 0.7700000000000001, 0.7700000000000001]
```

The same variance was seen with two items in the bank
(`0.7700000000000001` vs `0.7699999228395211`) and with one item in the bank
across 8 runs (no divergence seen there, so a single-item bank may not trigger
it).

## Impact

- Retrieval is not reproducible for identical stored content: the importance
  boost multiplies the fused score, so the same query against two equivalent
  stores can return slightly different `score` values.
- Near-tied hits can swap order between runs, which makes ranking regressions
  hard to tell apart from noise.
- Any test that asserts an exact `admission_score`, an exact fused score, or an
  exact hit order against seeded data can flake.

## Notes

Found incidentally while comparing `recall` output between two builds. It is not
caused by that work and was not fixed there; the retrieval crates involved were
untouched.
issues.title: Identical `remember` input stores a different `admission_score` about 1 run in 10

issues.body:
## Summary

Two tests in `crates/clio-compliance` intermittently fail when they run at the
same time in the same test process. Both build their exported bundle at the
same temp path, then fail while parsing that file.

## Cause

`unique()` in `crates/clio-compliance/src/import_fixture.rs:93` builds temp
names as `{prefix}-{nanos}-{pid}`. Inside one process the pid is the same, so
two calls that land in the same nanosecond clock tick return the same name.
`write_bundle` (`crates/clio-compliance/src/import_fixture.rs:439-441`) then
writes different bundle JSON to that single path with a non-atomic
`std::fs::write`. When two writes interleave, the file ends up as one document
followed by the tail of the other, so the `serde_json::from_str` call in
`crates/clio-compliance/src/import.rs:122-127` reports `trailing characters` at
the surviving document's length plus one.

The sibling module `crates/clio-compliance/src/stats_tests.rs:30-35` already
avoids this with an `AtomicU64` counter and has a
`unique_values_are_distinct_for_adjacent_calls` test.

## Reproduction

`make check` (full workspace gate); the failing suite is
`cargo test --locked -p clio-compliance --lib`.

Observed once while a second `cargo test` run shared the machine. Both tests
pass when run alone, and 65 further isolated repeats of the suite (40 plain,
25 under extra CPU load) did not reproduce it.

Actual output from the failing run:

    test result: FAILED. 108 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.84s

    ---- import_restore_tests::belief_trajectory_dedupes_and_appends stdout ----
    panicked at crates/clio-compliance/src/import_restore_tests.rs:168:10:
    belief import succeeds: AmError { code: InvalidArgument, message: "bundle JSON invalid: trailing characters at line 1 column 1055" }

    ---- import_restore_tests::belief_dry_run_rejects_below_threshold_without_writes stdout ----
    panicked at crates/clio-compliance/src/import_restore_tests.rs:264:10:
    dry-run belief reject succeeds: AmError { code: InvalidArgument, message: "bundle JSON invalid: trailing characters at line 1 column 1055" }

Both tests pass in isolation:

    cargo test --locked -p clio-compliance --lib -- import_restore_tests::belief_trajectory_dedupes_and_appends import_restore_tests::belief_dry_run_rejects_below_threshold_without_writes --exact
    test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

## Expected

Each test reads the bundle it wrote.

## Impact

False red on the workspace gate. No product or data effect; the collision only
touches test temp files.

## Proposed fix

Give `unique()` a process-wide counter (`AtomicU64`, as `stats_tests.rs` does),
or create the temp bundle as a create-new unique file so two writers can never
share one path.
issues.title: Test flake: clio-compliance import tests collide on a shared temp bundle path

issues.body:
## Summary

`http_bind::tests::occupied_port_advances_to_next_free` intermittently fails with a port-in-use panic on an unchanged tree. The test picks a free successor port by binding and immediately dropping a probe, then rebinds that port later with no retry. Any other process that binds the probed port in the gap makes the test fail.

Found incidentally while running `make check` on unrelated documentation changes. Not fixed here.

## Reproduction

Run the full CLI binary test suite:

```bash
cargo test --locked -p clio --bin clio
```

It is intermittent, not deterministic. It was observed once while a second test run of this repository was executing on the same machine (both runs bind ephemeral ports). Running only the module passes:

```bash
cargo test --locked -p clio --bin clio -- http_bind::tests
```

Observed failure (full-suite run):

```text
---- http_bind::tests::occupied_port_advances_to_next_free stdout ----

thread 'http_bind::tests::occupied_port_advances_to_next_free' panicked at crates/clio-lib/src/http_bind_tests.rs:79:62:
binds the next free port: Custom { kind: AddrInUse, error: "no free port in 64178-64179 on 127.0.0.1; stop the other listener or pass --bind HOST:PORT" }

test result: FAILED. 570 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Immediately after the failure, port 64179 was free again, and the same test passed in isolation (`7 passed; 0 failed`).

## Expected result

The test binds the successor port it probed and passes.

## Actual result

`bind_first_free(localhost(), busy..=free)` at `crates/clio-lib/src/http_bind_tests.rs:79` finds the whole `busy..=free` range in use and the test panics.

## Mechanism

`occupied_with_free_next` (`crates/clio-lib/src/http_bind_tests.rs:111`) holds `busy` with a listener, proves `busy + 1` is free by binding it, and drops that probe listener at `crates/clio-lib/src/http_bind_tests.rs:120` before returning. The successor port is therefore unowned between the probe drop and the rebind at line 79, so another process can take it.

The sibling test `explicit_address_is_honored` (`crates/clio-lib/src/http_bind_tests.rs:31`) hits the same window and mitigates it with a 100-attempt retry loop, with a comment saying a just-dropped probe port can be taken by a parallel thread. `occupied_port_advances_to_next_free` has no retry.

## Impact

Intermittent false failure of `cargo test -p clio --bin clio` and `make check` whenever another process binds the probed port, for example when two pipeline runs share a machine. A rerun costs several minutes and the failure looks like a real regression. Test-only; no product behavior is affected.

## Proposed fix

Retry the probe-and-bind in `occupied_port_advances_to_next_free`, or make `occupied_with_free_next` keep the successor probe listener open and hand it back instead of dropping it, matching the mitigation already used by `explicit_address_is_honored`.

Found incidentally and not fixed.
issues.title: Test flake: `occupied_port_advances_to_next_free` fails when another process takes the probed port

issues.body:
## Summary

The reserved top-level CLI surfaces that parse flags with the lenient `parse_flags` extractor ignore unknown flags. `clio status --bogus`, `clio ops diagnose --bogus`, and `clio mcp schema-export --bogus` all run normally and exit 0. The shared hand-rolled parser (`crates/clio-lib/src/cli_args.rs`) rejects unknown flags with a usage error (exit 2), and `clio status` itself documents exit 2 for usage errors, so behavior differs by surface.

## Reproduction

```
cargo build --locked --bin clio
./target/debug/clio status --backend sqlite --db sqlite::memory: --bogus; echo $?
./target/debug/clio status --backend sqlite --db sqlite::memory: -x; echo $?
./target/debug/clio ops diagnose --backend sqlite --db sqlite::memory: --bogus; echo $?
./target/debug/clio mcp schema-export --bogus; echo $?
```

Actual (sanitized):

```
clio status: healthy
...
0
clio status: healthy
...
0
0
{"catalog_hash":"fnv1a64:...","format":"am_tool_schema_pack",...}
0
```

## Expected

Each invocation should fail closed with a usage error and exit code 2, the same as `clio recall q --bogus` does (`unknown flag `--bogus``), or at minimum reject the unknown flag instead of ignoring it.

## Actual

Unknown flags are silently stored or skipped and the command proceeds with defaults. Relevant code: `crates/clio-lib/src/main.rs:148-160` (`parse_flags` accepts any `--name` and skips tokens that do not start with `--`); `crates/clio-lib/src/status_cli.rs:113-121` (only known keys are read); the same extractor is used at `crates/clio-lib/src/ops_cli.rs:57`, `crates/clio-lib/src/mcp_cli.rs:47`, `crates/clio-lib/src/compose_cli.rs:49`, and `crates/clio-lib/src/retention_cli.rs:39`.

## Impact

A typo or unsupported flag on a health, ops, compose, mcp, or retention command is silently accepted and the command runs with defaults. Scripts and agents cannot tell a malformed invocation from a valid one, which is the opposite of the shared parser's fail-closed contract and contradicts `clio status`'s documented "2 usage" exit code.

## Notes

Found incidentally while working on CLI output flag handling; not fixed because it is outside that task's scope. A fix needs a per-surface known-flag list (or routing these surfaces through `cli_args::parse`), which is a design change beyond the incidental report.
issues.title: Reserved CLI surfaces ignore unknown flags and exit 0 instead of a usage error

issues.body:
## Summary

The sidecar/provider transport accepts `http://` for **any host**, not just loopback, and then attaches the provider API key as a bearer token. Config validation requires only that the URL be a string — there is no scheme restriction, no host restriction, and no warning for a non-loopback plaintext endpoint.

An operator who points `extract.url` (or `embed.url` / `rerank.url`) at a remote `http://` endpoint sends a long-lived provider API key **and** the memory text being embedded or extracted in cleartext.

**Severity: Low–Medium.** It requires an operator configuration choice, but a "local sidecar" default is being silently extended to arbitrary remote hosts with no guard.

## Affected code

| Location | Role |
|---|---|
| `crates/clio-index/src/http.rs:71-80` | `HttpEndpoint::parse` accepts `http://` for any host, not only loopback |
| `crates/clio-index/src/http.rs:252` | embed request attaches `authorization: Bearer {key}` |
| `crates/clio-index/src/http.rs:285` | health-probe path attaches the same header |
| `crates/clio-config/src/config/validate.rs:254-266` | `embed.url` / `rerank.url` / `extract.url` validated as string only |

## Reproduction

Bytes captured off a socket by the real client:

```
[parse] accepted remote http:// -> host=api.vendor.example.com port=80 path=/v1/embed

[wire]   POST /v1/embed HTTP/1.1
[wire]   accept-encoding: gzip
[wire]   content-length: 48
[wire]   user-agent: ureq/3.4.2
[wire]   host: 127.0.0.1:60360
[wire]   content-type: application/json
[wire]   authorization: Bearer sk-live-VENDORKEY-abc123
[wire]
[wire]   {"input":"confidential memory text","model":"m"}

[wire] provider API key appeared in cleartext on the wire: true
[wire] confidential request payload in cleartext           : true
```

Real code exercised: `clio_index::HttpEndpoint::parse`, `clio_index::post_json`.

## Impact

- **Secret disclosure.** The provider API key traverses the network in cleartext and in the cleartext request body.
- **Content disclosure.** The memory text being embedded or extracted is readable by any network observer.
- **Integrity.** The request can be read and modified in transit, so an on-path attacker can alter the embedding/extraction input or response.

## Note on scope

The response side is handled well: `read_capped` (`crates/clio-index/src/http.rs:209-233`) enforces a 64 MiB cap, and TLS verification is in place for `https://` with optional custom root CA. This issue is specifically about the *request* side and the missing scheme/host guard.

## Proposed fix

- Require `https://` for any non-loopback host.
- Warn — or refuse — on `http://` to a remote address at configuration time, mirroring the loopback-only rule the MCP HTTP bind already enforces at `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:90-96`.

That rule is a good precedent: the codebase already understands that a non-loopback listener needs protection. The same reasoning applies to an outbound non-loopback plaintext endpoint.

## Related

- #20 — plaintext triple SPO survives compliance erasure (the at-rest counterpart to this in-transit gap)
issues.title: [security:low] Provider API key and memory payload sent over cleartext http:// to any host

issues.body:
## Summary

The MCP HTTP transport spawns **one `std::thread::spawn` per accepted connection**, with no cap, no pool, and **no read timeout** on the stream. A connection that sends no bytes holds its thread indefinitely. Threads accumulate without limit, and the thread is allocated *before* any authentication or origin check runs.

**Severity: Low** for the documented loopback default, **Medium** if the listener is exposed.

## Affected code

| Location | Role |
|---|---|
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:99-106` | `std::thread::spawn` per accepted connection, no cap and no pool |
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:111-124` | `handle_conn` blocks in `read_request`; no read timeout is ever set on the stream |
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:151-209` | the blocking read loop itself |
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:165-189` | `MAX_BODY` bounds *completed* data but does nothing for an idle connection |
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:90-96` | non-loopback binds require a token — but the token is not needed to *occupy* a thread |

## Reproduction

```
[idle]    200 idle connections held open, none authenticated
[idle]    live threads on this host: 202
[serve]   after 200 idle conns, authorized request -> HTTP/1.1 200 in 3.4ms
[exhaust] connect() started failing after 14727 extra idle connections
[exhaust] authorized request now -> connect failed: Can't assign requested address
```

The server stops accepting new connections once ephemeral ports are exhausted.

Real code exercised: `clio_mcp::http::serve_with_listener`, `clio_mcp::runtime::McpState::open`, driving a real `tools/list` JSON-RPC request.

## Impact

Local or container-level denial of service. Not a privilege escalation.

## Accuracy notes

- Request bodies **are** capped at 10 MiB. The missing protection is the count and lifetime of threads, not body size.
- A non-loopback bind cannot start without a token (`http.rs:90-96`), but authentication runs *after* the thread is already allocated and blocked in `read`. A token is therefore not required to consume a thread.
- A valid-token holder doing this to themselves is self-DoS, not escalation.
- The realistic adversaries are an untrusted local process, or a container / reverse-proxy setup that publishes the loopback-bound port.

## Proposed fix

- Set read and write deadlines on the stream before parsing begins.
- Replace one-thread-per-connection with a bounded worker pool or a connection-count semaphore.

## Related

- #22 — the same root cause in the sync HTTP transport: hand-rolled HTTP server with no resource bounds. The two share a fix pattern and should probably be addressed together.
issues.title: [security:low] MCP HTTP transport spawns unbounded threads with no read timeout

issues.body:
## Summary

The sync server's HTTP framing loop grows its buffer **without any size cap**, and it runs **before** the authentication check. Because connections are handled **serially in the accept loop**, one unauthenticated client can occupy the single server slot while growing server memory — without ever presenting a token.

The MCP transport in the same workspace does this correctly: it enforces a 10 MiB `MAX_BODY` and returns 413 (`crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:37-38`, `:165-189`). The sync transport has no equivalent.

**Severity: Medium** when network-exposed, **Low** for the documented loopback default. Availability only — not an authorization bypass.

## Affected code

| Location | Role |
|---|---|
| `crates/clio-sync/src/http.rs:90-118` | `read_request` grows `buf` with no cap on the header block or the declared `Content-Length` |
| `crates/clio-sync/src/server.rs:173` | `read_request` is called **before** any auth decision |
| `crates/clio-sync/src/server.rs:181` | `authorized()` is checked only afterwards |
| `crates/clio-sync/src/server.rs:151-170` | `serve_loop` handles each connection serially in the accept loop, no thread spawn |
| `crates/clio-sync/src/server.rs:160-162` | 5s `set_read_timeout`, whose result is discarded |

The read loop only terminates when it has seen `\r\n\r\n` **and** read `Content-Length` bytes. An attacker controls both of those conditions.

## Reproduction

Against a real `sync_serve` with a token configured:

```
[baseline] authorized empty push -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
[flood] one connection buffered ~11 MiB in 5.117s with no header terminator
[hol]   legitimate request during one stalled connection: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
[hol]   legitimate request waited 11.130s
[after] server recovered -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK in 55.172ms
```

Real code exercised: `clio_sync::server::sync_serve`, `clio_store::SqliteStore::open_in_memory`, `clio_store::LocalDevKms`.

## Impact

A pre-authentication denial of service against the sync peer. An attacker who has **no token** can still occupy the only accept slot for the duration of the read window, stalling every other client.

## Accuracy notes

- The 5-second `set_read_timeout` is a **per-read** timeout, not a total request deadline. A client sending one byte every few seconds holds the connection indefinitely.
- The result of `set_read_timeout` is discarded, so a failure to apply it is silent.
- The default bind is loopback, so exposure requires an operator binding to a LAN or `0.0.0.0` with a token.
- The ~11 MiB figure is specific to this host's speed. The unbounded-growth property is structural; the exact number is not portable.

## Proposed fix

- Cap the header block size and reject a declared `Content-Length` above a sane maximum, mirroring the MCP transport's `MAX_BODY`.
- Add a **total** request deadline, not just a per-read timeout.
- Replace the serial accept loop with a bounded worker pool or a connection semaphore.

## Related

- #23 — the same root cause in the MCP HTTP transport: hand-rolled HTTP server with no resource bounds. The two share a fix pattern and should probably be addressed together.
issues.title: [security:medium] Sync server buffers requests unboundedly before authenticating, and handles connections serially

issues.body:
## Summary

`sync_push` optionally encrypts outgoing content with XChaCha20-Poly1305. The nonce is derived from the **wall clock and the plaintext length**. It contains no random input.

Reusing a (key, nonce) pair under this AEAD repeats the ChaCha20 keystream and the Poly1305 one-time key. The code at `crates/clio-sync/src/crypto.rs:76-106`:

```rust
let nanos = std::time::SystemTime::now()
    .duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH)
    .map_or(0, |d| d.as_nanos());
let digest = clio_store::sha256_hex(
    format!("{nanos}|{}", plaintext.len()).as_bytes(),
    "am-sync-nonce",
);
let nonce_bytes: [u8; 24] = digest.as_bytes()[..24]
    .try_into()
    .expect("24-byte nonce slice");
```

A source comment at `crypto.rs:77-78` already acknowledges the shortcut:

> `// ponytail: XChaCha nonce from hashed time+length, not a CSPRNG pull;`
> `// switch to OsRng at the first cryptanalytic or throughput concern.`

This issue is that the switch has not happened, and the concern has arrived.

**Severity: Medium**, rising to **High** against a malicious sync peer or an on-path observer holding one known plaintext.

## Affected code

| Location | Role |
|---|---|
| `crates/clio-sync/src/crypto.rs:76-106` | `seal()` derives the nonce; no counter, lock, random source, or duplicate check |
| `crates/clio-sync/src/client_feed.rs:217-226` | `content_for()` calls `seal()` once per outgoing mutation |
| `crates/clio-lib/src/sync_cli.rs:238-239` | `--sync-key` / `CLIO_SYNC_KEY` enables the cipher |
| `crates/clio-mcp/src/sync_tools.rs:157` | MCP `sync_key` argument builds the cipher |

`SyncCipherKey::from_secret` (`crypto.rs:61-70`) derives the same key deterministically on every process, so the collision space is shared across every client using that secret.

## Reproduction

Calling the real `SyncCipherKey::seal` 240,000 times across 8 threads under a single key:

```
[seal] 240000 seals across 8 threads -> 43932 distinct nonces
[seal] nonce values reused = 42793, worst single-nonce reuse = 8
[leak] msg ct#13836 XOR msg ct#43800 == pt#13836 XOR pt#43800 : true
[leak] recovered pt#13836 with NO key                 : {"w":0,"i":0013836}
[leak] recovery matches the true plaintext         : true
```

Separately, the nonce of a live ciphertext was reproduced **offline** from `(clock, length)` in 200/200 trials with no key material:

```
[predict] nonce reproduced offline in 200/200 trials = 200/200
```

## Impact

An observer holding two ciphertexts under a reused nonce learns the XOR of the plaintexts. One known plaintext then yields full recovery of the other.

A known plaintext is plausible here: the protocol already transmits `content_hash` in the clear (`crates/clio-sync/src/client_feed.rs:236-240`), so a guess can be validated without the key. Low-entropy fields and short items make this easy.

The sync server is a realistic observer. It stores client ciphertext verbatim, by design — it is meant to be server-blind.

## Accuracy notes

Three points that are commonly misread, stated precisely:

- The 24-byte nonce is **24 ASCII hex characters**, not 24 raw digest bytes. `sha256_hex` returns hex text, so this is 96 bits of hash output, not 192.
- The XOR identity holds for the ciphertext **body**, not the full `ciphertext_b64` value, which appends the 16-byte Poly1305 tag.
- A single CLI `push()` is sequential. Reuse arises from the concurrency that is genuinely present: MCP HTTP serves each connection on its own thread (`crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:99-106`), and multiple client processes or devices share one `sync_key`.

Nonce **predictability alone is not a vulnerability** — nonces are public values and may legitimately be counter-based. The defect is reuse. Poly1305 key reuse also opens a forgery path, but only with further known or chosen message-tag pairs; a passive observer holding two opaque ciphertexts does not automatically gain arbitrary forgery.

## Proposed fix

Draw 24 **raw** bytes from `OsRng` per seal, or use a persisted per-key counter that is safe across processes.

Add a test asserting nonce uniqueness under concurrency. The existing test at `crates/clio-sync/src/crypto_tests.rs:58-65` only checks that two sequential seals differ, which passes merely because the clock ticked — it does not exercise the actual failure mode.

While there: `sha256_hex(secret, "am-sync-key")` in `from_secret` is a single unsalted SHA-256 with no key-derivation function. Acceptable for a high-entropy machine secret, weak for a human passphrase.

## Related

- #20 — plaintext triple SPO survives compliance erasure (the at-rest counterpart)
issues.title: [security:medium] Sync AEAD nonce derived from wall clock and plaintext length, not a CSPRNG

issues.body:
## Summary

A knowledge triple's subject, predicate, and object are stored as **plaintext** in the `triples` table, even though the identical content is correctly DEK-sealed inside the carrier item's `content_ciphertext`.

The compliance erasure path never references the `triples` table. So a verified data-subject erasure destroys the DEK — correctly rendering the carrier item unreadable — while the same content sits in the clear in a neighbouring table and remains fully readable with no key.

The result: the system writes a tombstone, passes its own DEK-destruction verification probe, and records the erasure as successful, while the content is still readable. That is a false attestation of erasure in the project's own audit trail.

**Severity: High.** Confidentiality loss at rest plus a compliance/erasure failure.

## Affected code

| Location | Role |
|---|---|
| `sql/001_core.sql:236-238` | `triples.subject`, `triples.predicate`, `triples.object` are plain `text NOT NULL` columns |
| `crates/clio-store/src/sqlite_triple.rs:158-186` | inserts the SPO verbatim into those columns |
| `crates/clio-store/src/postgres_triple.rs` | same insert on the Postgres backend |
| `crates/clio-store/src/sqlite_erase_purge.rs:113-161` | erase purges `item_embeddings`, `index_pending`, `items_fts`, `assoc_edges`, `memtree_nodes` — **no statement against `triples`** |
| `crates/clio-store/src/postgres_erase.rs` | same omission on Postgres |

The only `DELETE FROM triples` anywhere in the workspace is test fixture code at `crates/clio-store/src/pg_ops_tests.rs:90`.

## The content is sealed elsewhere, so this is an inconsistency, not a design choice

`crates/clio-write/src/triple.rs:246-276` builds a carrier item whose `snapshot` and `gist` contain the same SPO triple. That item **is** correctly sealed under the data-subject DEK. The identical content therefore exists twice: sealed in `items.content_ciphertext`, and in the clear in `triples`.

The `beliefs` table already documents the correct pattern in its own DDL comment at `sql/001_core.sql:335-337`:

> The proposition CONTENT is sealed under the subject DEK; only the normalized identity key and structure are plaintext (§7.4 field-level encryption).

The `triples` table applies the opposite treatment to the same kind of content. Its `subject`/`predicate`/`object` are proposition content, not bi-temporal structure.

## Reachability

`triple_add` is a first-class MCP tool.

```
crates/clio-mcp/src/write_tools.rs:279   fn triple_add(state, args)
crates/clio-mcp/src/write_tools.rs:315   clio_write::triple::triple_add(...)
crates/clio-write/src/triple.rs:210       store.commit_triple_add(admitted, &e, ...)
```

`subject`, `predicate`, and `object` are free-text arguments supplied by whatever model or user invokes the tool, so real deployments will contain whatever people type there.

## Reproduction

Driven through the real MCP tool handler, then the real erasure API. A scratch crate linked against the workspace crates by path; no repository files were modified.

```
[mcp] triple_add over the real MCP handler -> ok=true
[mcp] triples rows now: 1
[mcp]   service:hunter2Correct | runs_on | host:db-hunter2Correct.internal:5432

[erase] erase_subject ok: 1 tombstone(s) written
[erase] carrier item now: unreadable (ErasedSubject)
[erase] triples rows surviving erase: 1
[erase]   subject = service:hunter2Correct
[erase]   object  = host:db-hunter2Correct.internal:5432
[erase]   contains the secret: true
```

Real code exercised: `clio_mcp::runtime::McpState::open`, `clio_mcp::protocol::McpHandler::handle_frame`, `clio_store::SqliteStore`, `clio_store::LocalDevKms::open_persistent`, `SubjectEraseSpec` / `erase_subject`.

A second run confirmed the plaintext is present in the raw `.db` bytes on disk, and that `list_triples` returns the SPO with **no DEK present at all**.

## Impact

**Confidentiality.** Anyone with read access to the database file, a backup, a volume snapshot, or a stolen disk reads every triple in cleartext. The per-subject DEK provides no protection for this content.

**Compliance.** An erasure request is recorded as successful — tombstone written, DEK destroyed, verification probe passes — while the subject's content remains readable.

## Proposed fix

Decide the storage shape explicitly, then implement it.

- **Preferred:** seal the SPO under the subject DEK and retain only a normalized identity key in plaintext, matching the `beliefs` table design and its DDL comment.
- **Alternative:** add `triples` to the erasure purge in both `sqlite_erase_purge.rs` and `postgres_erase.rs`.

Either way, add a regression test asserting that `triple_add` followed by `erase_subject` leaves no readable copy of the content.

Note the related latent issue in the MemTree persistence primitive: `upsert_memtree_node` has no production caller today (only test fixtures), so `memtree_nodes.summary_gist` is currently a plaintext column with no reachable writer. Worth a guard test before anyone wires that primitive up.

## Related

- #24 — provider key and memory payload sent over cleartext `http://` (the in-transit counterpart to this at-rest gap)
issues.title: [security:high] Plaintext triple SPO survives compliance erasure (DEK shredded, content still readable)

issues.body:
## Summary

When any existing item row in a bank has a sealed body that fails AEAD authentication (for example one flipped character inside `items.content_ciphertext`), every new `remember`/`store` write to that bank fails with `factor_unavailable: content decryption failed`, even though the new write does not touch the unreadable row. The admission novelty factor appears to decrypt neighbor rows and propagates the decrypt error instead of skipping the unreadable row.

Found incidentally while verifying a separate read-listing fix; not fixed in that change.

## Reproduction

1. Create a data dir and store one item:

   ```
   CLIO_DATA_DIR=/tmp/repro clio remember "tamper probe note" --category task_spec --bank demo --actor agent --output json
   # ok
   ```

2. Copy the data dir. In the copy, open `clio.db` and flip one character inside the `ciphertext_b64` value of the stored `items.content_ciphertext` envelope (keeping base64 validity so the envelope still parses; this breaks AEAD authentication).

3. On the tampered copy:

   ```
   CLIO_DATA_DIR=/tmp/repro-copy target/debug/clio remember "write probe after corruption" \
     --category task_spec --bank demo --actor agent --output json
   {"code":"factor_unavailable","message":"factor_unavailable: content decryption failed","ok":false}  # exit 1
   ```

4. Control: the same `remember` command against the untouched copy succeeds (`ok: true`, exit 0).

Also reproduced in-process: with a file-backed database opened under a fresh key store, `store` for a new item fails with `factor_unavailable: no DEK for subject `<another subject>`' while an old sealed row is unreadable.

## Expected result

A write whose own inputs are valid should succeed (or report a targeted, self-explanatory failure). An unreadable neighbor row should at most degrade that item's novelty contribution (or skip it with a warning), not fail every write in the bank. Direct reads of the unreadable item (`clio get <id>`) correctly still report `forbidden: content decryption failed`; the listing tool (`clio inspect`) already skips unreadable rows.

## Actual result

Any create against the bank exits 1 with `{"code":"factor_unavailable","message":"factor_unavailable: content decryption failed","ok":false}`. A data dir with a single corrupted (or key-mismatched) row becomes write-hostile for the whole bank.

## Impact

One damaged or key-orphaned row blocks all ingestion into the affected bank, which is worse than the read side (listing still works, single reads still report the row's own error). No data loss occurs, but recovery requires repairing or removing the unreadable row first.

## Notes

- Error surfaced from the store decrypt layer (`clio-store` KMS decrypt maps AEAD authentication failure to `ErrorCode::Forbidden`, message `content decryption failed`), wrapped as `factor_unavailable` by the admission factor path (see `clio-admission` novelty scoring / `clio-mcp` write tools).
- The behavior is present on the current master build (`make compile`, `cargo test --workspace` green apart from this scenario).
issues.title: One unreadable ciphertext row blocks all new writes to the bank with factor_unavailable during admission
